media.alt: AKU hosts international workshop on malnutrition in South Asia malnutrition results in Eeonomic loss worldwide - US$ 8.7 billion due to reducesed labour productivity

content.text: The Aga Khan University (AKU) will hold a two-day workshop on "Maternal and Foetal Malnutrition and Human Development in South Asia" on October 28 and 29, 1999. This will be followed by a seminar on ''Women and Nutrition in South Asia: Issues and Strategies for Change" on October 30. Numerous issues such as maternal nutrition, low birth weight and reproductive health will be discussed by eminent speakers and experts from Pakistan and abroad. Malnutrition during childhood and adult life reduces school performance, labour productivity and general economic growth with long term effects of reduced intellectual capacity and the risk of chronic diseases. Economic losses worldwide from reduced labour productivity alone are US$ 8.7 billion. Clearly, it is an issue that deserves urgent attention in the South Asian context.

Over 500 million people world-wide, do not get enough food to lead healthy and productive lives. The majorities of these are poor and live in South Asia and Africa. In addition, each year about 24 million children are born underweight, largely due to malnutrition in women during pregnancy and in early life. About 5 million infants are unable to cope with this malnutrition and low birth weight and die before they reach their fifth birthday. Furthermore, half of the 170 million malnourished preschool children are found in just three countries, Bangladesh, India and Pakistan.

A crucial determinant of a newborn's survival and healthy start in life is the mother's health and nutritional status. In Pakistan, 20-40 percent of women are underweight and 40-50 percent suffer from anaemia. As a result, 25-30 percent of Pakistani infants are born with low birth weights (less than 2.5 kilograms). These statistics have remained static for several decades. Not only are these women and children more prone to infections and early death, but also grow up as malnourished children, adolescents and adults, who are unable to realize their full physical and intellectual potential.

South Asia has the worst malnutrition levels in the world, contributing to a vicious cycle of poor growth from generation to generation. Malnourished mothers are more likely to have low birth weight babies who if female, will be predisposed to produce weak infants. This cycle is very evident in patriarchal South Asian societies, where cultural biases towards boys often means that the girl child is less well cared for, being fed last and getting the least to eat. The mortality rate for girls and women is therefore much higher than for men in South Asia. For every 100 men there are only 94 women who survive. According to these figures, 74 million women who should be alive in South Asia today are missing.

The international workshop and seminar hosted by AKU will seek to develop a framework for maternal and child care and nutritional interventions to bring about change in the short and long term in South Asia.
